summary: Documents experience with OSPF version 2, including interoperability testing, field experience, simulations, and the state of implementations. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1246 is a report on how the OSPF routing protocol performed when it was put into real networks and tested against routers from other vendors. It records the tests, the deployments, the measurements and the mistakes that were found and fixed.

questions: what experience was there with ospf v2
how did ospf v2 perform in real networks
what was the convergence time for ospf v2
how much bandwidth did ospf use compared to rip
was ospf v2 ready for standardization
subtitle: What happened when OSPF was put into real networks and tested against other vendors.

tldr.problem: OSPF could not advance to Draft Standard status until the Internet community had evidence that independent implementations work together and that the protocol runs in production.
tldr.mechanism: This report collects that evidence: interoperability sessions with five implementations, three live deployments with their measured convergence times, the OSPF Management Information Base, the authentication design and a simulation study.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that specifies no standard, and it reaches a clear verdict: no OSPF protocol problems were found in operational deployments, and the hard part turned out to be OSPF and RIP working side by side.

facts.label: Document type
facts.value: Informational RFC, second of two OSPF reports

today: RFC 1246 is an Informational RFC that specifies no standard. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It was written to support OSPF's move to Draft Standard status and describes OSPF Version 2, which the report itself records as being specified in RFC 1247.

sections.title: What This Report Is For
sections.content:
RFC 1246 is the second of two reports on the OSPF protocol, and it exists because the IAB and the IESG require such reports before an Internet routing protocol can advance to Draft Standard status. OSPF is a TCP/IP routing protocol designed to be used inside an Autonomous System, which makes it an Interior Gateway Protocol. At the time of writing OSPF was designated as a Proposed Standard. Version 1 of the protocol was published in RFC 1131; Version 2 has been developed since and is documented in RFC 1247, with the differences between the two versions listed in Appendix F of that RFC. Everything in this report concerns Version 2 unless it says otherwise.

The requirements the report has to meet are stated in the introduction. The specification must be well written enough that independent, interoperable implementations can be built from the specification alone, without consulting the original developers. A Management Information Base must be written for the protocol, and be in the standardization process, though not necessarily at the same level as the protocol itself. The security architecture must be set forth explicitly, with mechanisms for authenticating routing messages and possibly other forms of protection. Two or more interoperable implementations must exist, at least two of them written independently. There must be evidence that all features of the protocol have been tested running between at least two implementations, including that the security features have been shown to work and that the mechanisms really do provide the intended protection. And there must be significant operational experience: a moderate number of routers in a moderately complex topology, part of the operational Internet, with all significant features exercised, and, for an interior protocol, both interior and exterior routes carried unless some other mechanism provides the exterior routes.

The rest of the report then documents how OSPF Version 2 meets each of those requirements. It notes that Version 1 was documented in RFC 1131 and Version 2 in RFC 1247, that the differences between them are relatively minor, and that the OSPF Working Group of the IETF met quarterly and held discussions on the ospf@trantor.umd.edu mailing list.
sections.plainLanguage: This report exists to answer one question: is OSPF good enough to become a standard? To answer it, the Internet community set six conditions in advance, including that two vendors must write working implementations independently and that the protocol must have been running in real networks. The rest of the report is the evidence.

sections.title: The OSPF Management Information Base
sections.content:
An OSPF Management Information Base has been published as RFC 1248, written by Rob Coltun and Fred Baker. The MIB appears on the management subtree as SMI standard-mib 13. It was originally developed by Rob Coltun at the University of Maryland under contract to Advanced Computer Communications, and a subset of his proposal was implemented to help their own development, which gives it a certain operational pedigree.

The MIB consists of a general variables group and ten tables: ospfGeneralGroup for general global variables, ospfAreaTable for area descriptions, ospfStubAreaTable for default metrics by type of service, ospfLsdbTable for the link state database, ospfAreaRangeTable for address range specifications, ospfHostTable for directly connected hosts, ospfIfTable for interface variables, ospfIfMetricTable for interface metrics by type of service, ospfVirtIfTable for virtual links, ospfNbrTable for non-virtual neighbours, and ospfVirtNbrTable for virtual neighbours.

By the standards of MIBs this one is large: 105 objects. Eleven define the group and the tables, ten define the entry within a table, seven are counters, six are gauges, and 68 are objects mandated by the OSPF Version 2 specification. Section D.2 of that specification lists a set of required statistics an implementation must maintain, and those statistics have been folded into the MIB. The counters and gauges are what let an operator evaluate how OSPF is performing in a live network, while most of the rest of the objects parameterise the many features OSPF gives the network administrator.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIB is the list of values a device exposes to a network manager. The OSPF MIB defines 105 of them: counters that show how the protocol is behaving, and settings that let an administrator tune how it behaves.

sections.title: How OSPF Authenticates Its Packets
sections.content:
In OSPF all protocol packet exchanges are authenticated. The OSPF packet header, which is common to every OSPF packet, carries a 16-bit Authentication type field and 64 bits of Authentication data. Each particular OSPF area must run a single authentication scheme, as indicated by the Authentication type field, although the authentication keys themselves are configured by the system administrator on a per-network basis.

When a router receives an OSPF packet it first checks that the packet indicates the correct Authentication type. It then authenticates the packet by running a verification algorithm whose inputs are the configured authentication key, the 64 bits of Authentication data and the rest of the OSPF packet data. The precise algorithm is dictated by the Authentication type. Packets that fail the algorithm are dropped, and the failure is recorded in a variable that a manager can read through the MIB.

At the time of writing there were few authentication types in use. Type 0 means no authentication is performed. Type 1 is a simple, clear password. Types 2 to 255 are reserved for assignment by the IANA, and anything above 255 is available for local, per-Autonomous-System definition.
sections.plainLanguage: Every OSPF packet is checked before it is believed. The check uses a key that the administrator sets on each network, and the header says which kind of check to run. A packet that fails the check is thrown away and the failure is counted.

sections.title: Operational Experience in Three Networks
sections.content:
OSPF Version 1 began to be deployed on the Internet in the Spring of 1990. The results were reported to the ospf-tests mailing list, and no protocol bugs were found in that first deployment, although several additional features turned out to be desirable. Those features were added in Version 2.

The report focuses on three visible systems. The NASA Science Internet (NSI) is a multiprotocol network supporting DECnet and TCP/IP, whose mission is to provide reliable high-speed communications to the NASA science community; it connects to the NSFNET, ESnet and MILNET and has international connections to Japan, Australia, New Zealand, Chile and several European countries. NSI was an initial Version 1 deployment site in April 1990 and had run Version 2 since 1 January 1991 with 15 routers, over a nationwide collection of serial lines with ethernets at hub sites. Many of its routers also speak RIP and/or EGP, and routes from those protocols are selectively imported into the OSPF system as externals, 496 of them at the time of writing, all imported as type 2 metrics. NSI also uses the external route tag to manage readvertisement: a route learned at one edge through EGP can be tagged with the number of the Autonomous System it came from, and that information is flooded to every other boundary router, which lets NSI apply transit policy at the granularity of Autonomous Systems rather than network numbers and so reduces its configuration burden. NSI has also experimented with stub areas to support routers with little memory.

BARRNet, the NSFNet regional network in Northern California, serves about 80 member sites between Sacramento and Monterey, over links from 9.6Kbps to full T1. Its OSPF system is fourteen Proteon routers forming a core, six of them redundantly connected into a ring, with member sites attached as stub connections. BARRNet was also an initial Version 1 site, in April 1990, and has run Version 2 since November 1990 with 14 routers. It imports a large number of external routes, 1816 of them, mostly T1 NSFNet routes, and imports them as type 1 metrics. It uses four stub OSPF areas to collapse subnet information; each is a single LAN with no OSPF routers in its interior. Its Version 1 deployment pointed to two features that were added to Version 2: a forwarding address in external link state advertisements, which removed the extra hops that occurred when only two routers exchanged EGP information with the NSS, and stub areas, which let OSPF run on routers with too little memory to hold all of BARRNet's external routes.

OARnet, the Ohio Academic Resources Network, was established in 1987 to give the state access to the CRAY at the Ohio Supercomputer Center and has grown into a network supporting higher education across Ohio. It has run OSPF Version 1 since 15 October 1990 with 14 routers, 29 sites connected directly to the backbone, all 13 OSPF routers acting as autonomous system boundary routers, 40 OSPF internal routes and about 120 routes imported from RIP. One router, OAR1, runs EGP on the DMZnet side and OSPF and RIP on the backbone, is configured to generate a default route when EGP routes are available, and acts as an intermediary for all of the network's RIP-centric routers. OARnet uses the event logging system on its Proteon routers to send traps about interesting routing events to an SNMP management station.

The measurements from these deployments are the reason to read the report. At NSI, a continuous ICMP ping was running when a link in its path was brought down, and the interrupted ping resumed in three seconds. On an NSI link with no users, so that all traffic on it was routing traffic, OSPF consumed many times less bandwidth than RIP.

OARnet's observations are more detailed. Three of its ten DS1 circuits are on digital microwave and tend to flap; the routers bring links and adjacencies up in about two seconds on average, routes fall back to alternate paths instantly, and whole blocks of routes cut over the moment the adjacencies form. The same site reports that its RIP routes would take about three to six minutes to cut over and would sometimes fail to return to the preferred paths, which it names as the prime motivation for switching to OSPF. In a detailed trace, bringing up the first adjacency after a router restart took about five seconds and subsequent adjacencies took less than a second; from the moment the first link came up to the moment the last was up was less than a minute. On the equivalent RIP test, OARnet needed three minutes to cut over to the slower fallback route and lost many packets, and the routes never returned to the faster paths even after waiting well over thirty minutes.
sections.plainLanguage: Three research networks ran OSPF in production and measured how quickly it recovered from a failure. The answer was seconds rather than minutes: one link failure restored traffic in three seconds, and routers rebuilt their adjacencies in about two seconds. The same networks reported that RIP took three to six minutes for the same job.

sections.title: Interoperability Testing Across Vendors
sections.content:
Three separate OSPF Version 2 interoperability testing sessions were held, and five implementations took part in at least one of them: 3com, ACC, Proteon and Wellfleet, and the publicly available implementation from the University of Maryland. The 3com implementation was wholly developed by 3com, took part in all three rounds, and was the only implementation of TOS routing; it is about 9000 lines of C. ACC's implementation is based on the University of Maryland code, took part in the last two rounds, and contains the only implementation of a precursor to the OSPF MIB, which it uses for monitoring and configuration; it is about 24,000 lines of C including its MIB code. Proteon's implementation was wholly developed by Proteon, took part in all three rounds, and is the only one with a significant amount of field experience; it is about 9500 lines of C. Wellfleet took part in all three rounds, and the University of Maryland implementation, written by Rob Coltun, has formed the basis for a number of commercial implementations and took part in the latest round; it is about 10,000 lines of C.

The three sessions grew each time. The first, at Proteon in the week of 25 September 1990, used six routers with 20 to 30 external routes and the 3com, Proteon and Wellfleet implementations. The second, at SURAnet in the week of 17 December 1990, used ten routers with 96 external routes and four implementations. The third, at 3com in the week of 4 February 1991, used sixteen routers with 400 external routes and all five implementations. The routers were interconnected using ethernet, serial lines carrying PPP or proprietary protocols, X.25 and 802.5 token ring, and problems were found through the routers' own error logs and through LAN protocol analysers capturing the packets.

Real defects turned up. In the first round, a window in the Database Description process allowed concurrently flooded MaxAge advertisements to prevent database synchronisation from completing, which required a change in the specification's handling of MaxAge link state advertisements, and the specification did not say how the Network Mask field should be set in external link state advertisements advertising the default destination. The second round found no problems in the OSPF protocol at all. In the third round, the specification did not say how the Network Mask field should be set in Hellos sent over virtual links, which made it hard to bring virtual links up between routers from different vendors, and it was not strict enough about how neighbours are identified on multi-access networks, which caused trouble when a router was restarted with the same IP address but a different OSPF Router ID.

The report's verdict is that the testing was very valuable. Many bugs were found and fixed in the implementations, some protocol problems were found and fixed, grey areas of the specification were cleared up, and implementations were made more robust in the face of unexpected behaviour from other implementations. All participants came away understanding the maxim be conservative in what you generate, and liberal in what you accept. The one area left mostly untested is the interaction between OSPF and other routing protocols such as RIP and EGP, especially between different vendors' routers, and the exchange of routing information between different protocols is named as an area of ongoing work and a candidate for future standardisation.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers from five different suppliers were wired together in three test sessions, each one bigger than the last. They found real defects in the protocol description and in the software, and all of them were fixed. What was left untested was how OSPF behaves next to RIP on routers from different suppliers.

sections.title: Simulation and the Gaps in Operational Testing
sections.content:
OSPF was also simulated by the Distributed Systems Research Group at the University of Maryland Baltimore County, under principal investigators Dr Deepinder P. Sidhu and Rob Coltun, with three graduate students. The group used a significantly enhanced version of the MIT network simulator, which is event driven and supports both point-to-point networks and ethernet links. It can simulate packet switches and hosts, can simulate internet behaviour under different traffic load distributions such as Poisson, normal, exponential and uniform, can take a specific topology or generate pseudo-random ones, and can simulate packet loss rates. Rob Coltun's OSPF implementation was incorporated into the simulator essentially unchanged, and the output could be displayed graphically using X windows, with any variable in the implementation under test monitored and statistical reports produced later from the log files.

The simulations used the two sample topologies from the OSPF specification, one an Autonomous System without areas and the other the same system with three areas and a virtual link, the 19-node hub topology from a BBN report, a large network of over 50 nodes all attached to a single ethernet, and a large network of over 50 nodes mixing ethernets and serial lines, pseudo randomly generated. The correctness of database synchronisation was verified by examining the nodes' link state databases and routing tables, multiple areas were tested, and convergence time was analysed as a function of link speed. Formal analysis was also carried out on the neighbour and interface state machines, and the Designated Router election algorithm was verified for certain sets of initial conditions.

The report is equally frank about what the live deployments did not cover. Multi-vendor deployments had not been tested operationally, because every deployment had used a single implementation. Regular OSPF areas, virtual links, non-broadcast networks and TOS routing had not been tested operationally either, but all of them had been covered in the interoperability sessions.

The conclusions are measured. All the basic features of the protocol had been exercised, very large link state databases had been deployed, and no OSPF protocol problems had been found in operational deployments. Most of the trouble in operational deployments came from the exchange of routes between OSPF and RIP. Many of those issues were ironed out on the ospf-tests mailing list, but the interaction between OSPF, RIP and EGP remained an active area of research when the report was written.
sections.plainLanguage: A research group also ran OSPF inside a network simulator, on topologies of up to more than fifty routers, to check that the databases stayed in step and to measure how quickly they converged. The report ends by listing what the live networks had not tried, and by saying that the only real difficulty found in production was OSPF talking to RIP.
